messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 59
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Professor
- Trauma Type: Trauma to a loved one
- Pcl5: 54

He is a 59-year-old African man who has spent most of his adult life in lecture halls, libraries, and faculty meetings, a professor known by colleagues for his discipline and by students for the care he puts into his teaching. He lives alone now, in a quiet apartment lined with books and marked by routines he once found stabilizing. When he speaks about what happened, he does so carefully, as if each detail must be lifted without breaking.

The event begins with his younger sister, the person he describes as “the one who kept the family stitched together.” She still lives in their home country while he has been abroad for many years building an academic career. They speak often, sometimes briefly between his classes, sometimes late at night when the time difference makes sleep inconvenient but conversation possible. He is used to being the brother who advises from afar—helping with school fees for nieces and nephews, discussing medical appointments, listening to the small dramas of home.

One evening, just after finishing a seminar, he notices several missed calls from a cousin. He feels an immediate tightening in his chest before he even answers. His sister has been attacked during a violent robbery at her home. At first the information comes in fragments: there was shouting, neighbors gathered, she was injured badly, she is being taken to a hospital. He remembers standing in his office with his bag still over one shoulder, unable to sit down, asking the same questions again because the answers do not hold. Over the next day he makes frantic calls, arranges money transfers, tries to reach doctors, tries to book travel. He feels the humiliating helplessness of distance—he can lecture on political violence, migration, and institutions, but he cannot get to his sister’s bedside fast enough.

She survives for several days. He flies home during that period and reaches the hospital exhausted and disoriented. What stays with him is not a single image but a set of sensations that seem burned into him: the smell of antiseptic mixed with sweat, the harsh hospital lights, the sound of his sister trying to breathe around pain. He sits beside her bed speaking softly, telling her things he cannot later remember. He watches her drift in and out of consciousness. When she dies, he experiences the moment as both loud and unreal—family members crying, bodies moving, hands touching him—while inside he feels abruptly blank, as if the world has gone mute.

In the months afterward, he returns to the university because the semester must continue. From the outside he appears functional. He prepares lectures, attends committee meetings, answers emails. But his life becomes narrower and strained. He avoids calling home unless necessary, because any unfamiliar number or delayed response fills him with dread. News reports about robberies, assaults, or hospital failures grip him with a physical jolt; he cannot look away, even as his heart races. At night he often sees his sister in the hospital bed just as he is falling asleep. Sometimes he dreams he is trying to reach her through endless airport corridors, his bags getting heavier while his phone slips from his hands. He wakes soaked in sweat, already tense, and checks his phone immediately.

His students notice small changes before his colleagues do. He loses his place mid-lecture when an ambulance siren passes outside. A student dropping a stack of books makes him flinch hard enough that the room goes quiet. He starts keeping his office door shut. He no longer lingers after class to chat. Once proud of his accessibility, he now feels irritated by interruptions and ashamed of that irritation. In meetings he sits near exits and scans faces when someone speaks too sharply. He tells himself these are signs of aging, fatigue, overwork—anything but injury.

He also carries a stubborn sense of guilt. He replays decisions obsessively: if he had pushed her to move, sent more money sooner, visited more often, answered the first missed call immediately. Intellectually he knows he did not cause the attack, but this knowledge does not touch the deeper conviction that he failed her in the moment she most needed protection. Being single seems to magnify the silence waiting for him at home. There is no one there to interrupt the long evenings when his mind circles back to the hospital, to the funeral, to his sister’s last days.

By the present time, nearly every part of his life is organized around preventing another shock or holding himself together after one. He sleeps lightly, keeps the television low, startles at footsteps in the corridor, and checks locks repeatedly before bed. He continues teaching because the classroom still gives him brief stretches of purpose, but even there he sometimes feels split in two—one part delivering a polished lecture, the other bracing for disaster. He describes himself now as a man who is “never fully where he is.” Even in his office, surrounded by books and the familiar rituals of academic life, some part of him remains in that hospital room, listening for his sister’s breathing.
